In Toledo, in the 1100s and 1200s, scholars translated Arabic books of science and philosophy into Latin, and later into Castilian. Their work is known as the Toledo School of Translators.

Castile took Toledo from the Muslims in 1085, and with it libraries and scholars of Arabic. Jews, Christians and converts worked together, often one reading the Arabic aloud in the local tongue and another writing it down in Latin. Gerard of Cremona alone translated over seventy works, among them Ptolemy's Almagest and works of Aristotle, al-Khwarizmi and Avicenna.

Through Toledo, Latin Europe recovered much of Greek learning and gained Arab mathematics, astronomy and medicine, which fed the new universities. In the 1200s King Alfonso X sponsored translations into Castilian. Toledo did for Europe what the House of Wisdom had done for Baghdad. See Spain and al-Andalus.
sum: In Toledo, in the 1100s and 1200s, scholars translated Arabic books of science and philosophy into Latin, and later into Castilian. Their work is known as the Toledo School of Translators.
